summary:
Eastern Visayas, six provinces in the eastern central Philippines, stands under the national framework of the Philippines, which applies uniformly across the region; the sources record no regional deviation from that framework, and the region is assessed at the national position.

Consensual same-sex relations are legal nationwide and no provision of national law criminalises a person for being transgender. Same-sex marriage is not recognised: the Family Code defines marriage as between a man and a woman. Transgender people cannot change their legal gender. The Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) forecloses an administrative birth-certificate sex change, leaving a court order as the only route, and the Supreme Court held in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan (2008) that legal gender may not be changed even after gender-affirming surgery.

No national anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation and gender identity exists. The SOGIE Equality Bill was filed in 1999 and has remained pending in Congress for roughly 25 years. Protections are sub-national: SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances operate at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels elsewhere in the country, and the parent framework records eight provinces and 32 cities and municipalities with such ordinances. Whether any local government inside Eastern Visayas has enacted one is not established by these sources.

Two executive measures exist on paper without effect. Executive Order 100, signed 17 December 2019, created a Diversity and Inclusion Program, and Executive Order 51 (2023) amended it to add a special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee; neither had been implemented as of 2025.

Public opinion bears on facilities access. A 2018 Social Weather Stations survey found 22% support for same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed transgender women's access to women's toilets, a position with direct consequences for restroom use in public buildings across the region.

Violence against trans women is documented and recent. Kierra Apostol, an 18-year-old trans woman, was found dead with signs of physical assault in a river in Peñablanca, Cagayan province on 23 June 2025, having been reported missing since 22 June; her mother reported the disappearance to local police. The chairperson of Bahaghari, the national LGBT alliance, called the killing part of a pattern of violence against Filipino trans women and renewed calls for the SOGIESC Equality Bill. The case occurred in Cagayan Valley rather than Eastern Visayas and is evidence of the national climate a visitor here moves through.
tangentialFactors:
Detention conditions apply to a visitor arrested in the region. Transgender women are held with male inmates according to birth sex; at Manila City Jail, arrivals to the male dormitory have their heads shaved, and safety is organised through inmate hierarchies and informal same-sex 'weddings' with male inmates rather than through policy. The Bureau of Jail Management and Penology's documented response at Davao City Jail is administrative segregation, transferring LGBT detainees in batches to the City Jail Annex 'to prevent abuse', alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens.

Schools are a further documented site of harm: a 2017 Human Rights Watch investigation recorded bullying and discrimination against gender-diverse students across Philippine schools while noting that law offered few remedies at the time.

A 2026 travel-risk assessment rates Manila 'Generally Safe' for LGBTQ+ travellers overall at 69 of 100 but scores trans travellers lower, at 62, in the 'Exercise Caution' band; no equivalent score exists for Eastern Visayas, and the national figure is the closest available comparator.

Sub-national protection is uneven across the country: the eight provinces with SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances are Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur and Iloilo, none of them in Eastern Visayas. Sectoral rules do apply nationally, including the Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (fine of PHP 20,000 to 40,000 and up to one year's penalty for SOGIE harassment), the Magna Carta of Women and the Safe Spaces Act (fines of PHP 1,000 to 10,000, up to 30 days' penalty and a sensitivity seminar), and the 2023 Code of Professional Responsibility barring lawyers from discriminating against clients on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity.
localsOnly:
Local LGBTQ political participation is recorded in the region. In Northern Samar, two of the province's 24 municipalities were reported (circa 2012) to be run by openly LGBTQ mayors, and Leyte is among the provinces listed as having LGBTQ elected officials.

Residents, as opposed to visitors, may also rely on whatever barangay, city, municipal or provincial anti-discrimination ordinances their own local government has enacted; the national SOGIE Equality Bill remains the unpassed instrument campaigners link to the absence of legislative remedy after killings of trans women, including two in June 2025.

Openly gay, bisexual and transgender service has been permitted in the armed forces since 2009 and 2017 respectively, with the uniform policy following the legal gender shown on the birth certificate, a rule that turns on documents rather than on identity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in this inventory states whether any of Eastern Visayas's six provinces or their cities and municipalities has enacted a SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinance. The ordinance counts cited (eight provinces, 32 cities and municipalities) name units outside the region, and the absence of a named Eastern Visayas ordinance in these sources is not evidence that none exists.

Unresolved: the sources are national rather than regional in origin, apart from the Northern Samar and Leyte political-participation datapoints. No regional enforcement data, no regional violence statistics and no regional travel-risk score are available here.

Unresolved: implementation status of Executive Order 100 and Executive Order 51 is stated only as 'not implemented as of 2025'; whether the special LGBTQIA+ affairs committee has convened since then is not sourced.

The 22% civil-union figure and the majority opposition to transgender women's use of women's toilets derive from a 2018 Social Weather Stations survey and are now several years old; no more recent national polling appears in this inventory.
